connections.feedback: Correct. Peaceful criticism of the government is at the heart of the First Amendment, even when others disagree.
The right belongs to individuals as well as the press. Ordinary people may speak, write and share opinions.
A person generally does not need a permit to express an opinion on a public sidewalk. Large events can have separate rules.
The right is not limited to government workers. It protects all people, including critics.

connections.feedback: Yes. In federal elections voting is a legal right. Many people also see it as a civic responsibility, which is a matter of values rather than law.
Defensible on the law. Legally, voting is a right and not required. The answer is incomplete, because it ignores the common view that voting is also a civic responsibility.
connections.notes: A strictly legal reading says right, not duty. Many civic educators also call it a responsibility. Both are reasonable, so this option is marked ambiguous.

Citizens do have a legal connection to elections. Voting is a right protected by law.
